title: THE WOMAN IN PHARAOH’S HOUSE WHO SAVED THE MAN GOD WOULD USE TO DESTROY PHARAOH’S POWER
paragraphs:
THE WOMAN IN PHARAOH’S HOUSE WHO SAVED THE MAN GOD WOULD USE TO DESTROY PHARAOH’S POWER
Before Moses ever stood before a king and said, “Let My people go,” an unnamed woman walked down to the Nile, heard a condemned baby crying, and made a decision that quietly changed the history of Israel.
There is something almost unbearable about the irony.
The Nile was supposed to be where Hebrew sons disappeared.
Instead, one little boy came out of it alive.
And the woman who helped make that possible was not standing among Israel’s oppressed families.
She came from Pharaoh’s own house.
Before Moses confronted Egypt...
before the plagues...
before the Passover...
before the sea opened...
before Israel walked toward freedom...
Moses was a helpless infant floating among the reeds.
He could not preach.
He could not perform a sign.
He could not confront Pharaoh.
He could not even save himself.
And somewhere between a murderous royal decree and the destiny God had prepared for this child, a woman saw a basket.
Then she heard a cry.
And everything changed.
Exodus tells us that Pharaoh had commanded concerning the Hebrew people:
“Every son that is born ye shall cast into the river, and every daughter ye shall save alive.”
— Exodus 1:22, KJV
Think about the horror hidden inside that sentence.
This was not merely politics.
Families were being torn apart.
Babies had become targets.
The river flowing through Egypt had been turned into an instrument of death.
Then Moses was born.
His mother hid him as long as she could. When hiding him became impossible, Exodus tells us that she prepared a small vessel, placed her son inside it, and laid it among the reeds by the riverbank.
The Hebrew wording deserves attention.
Exodus 2:3 calls the vessel a תֵּבָה — tevah.
That word is striking because the same Hebrew noun is used for Noah’s ark in Genesis.
Moses was not sailing a ship.
He was an infant placed inside a tiny ark.
A child surrounded by death...
carried in a vessel associated in Scripture with preservation through judgment.
But we should be careful here.
The text does not say Moses’ mother knew exactly how everything would unfold. Scripture does not invite us to invent details it never gives us.
What it does show us is a desperate mother doing what she could with the life entrusted to her.
And then Pharaoh’s daughter arrived.
“And the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself at the river; and her maidens walked along by the river’s side; and when she saw the ark among the flags, she sent her maid to fetch it.”
— Exodus 2:5, KJV
She opened it.
There was a baby inside.
Crying.
Exodus 2:6 records the moment:
“And when she had opened it, she saw the child: and, behold, the babe wept.”
Then Scripture gives us one of the most important details in the entire scene:
“And she had compassion on him...”
The Hebrew is:
וַתַּחְמֹל עָלָיו
vattaḥmol ʿalav
She had compassion on him.
She spared him.
She pitied him.
And she immediately recognized what she was looking at:
“This is one of the Hebrews’ children.”
She knew.
That changes everything.
This was not simply a woman rescuing a baby because she misunderstood his identity.
She recognized that he was Hebrew.
She knew the world into which he had been born.
She belonged to Pharaoh’s household, while Pharaoh had commanded that Hebrew sons be thrown into the Nile.
Yet standing beside that same Nile, she looked at one of those sons...
and compassion moved her.

We should not exaggerate what Scripture says. Exodus does not tell us everything Pharaoh’s daughter believed about Israel, Pharaoh, or Israel’s God at this point. It does not give us permission to manufacture a conversion testimony for her.
But it does tell us what she did.
She saw.
She recognized.
She had compassion.
And she acted.
Sometimes history turns on moments that do not look historic while they are happening.
A woman hears a baby crying.
A sister watches from a distance.
A mother waits somewhere with an aching heart.
A princess makes a decision.
Nobody standing on that riverbank could see the Red Sea yet.
Nobody could hear Pharaoh screaming through the future.
Nobody could see Sinai trembling.
Nobody could see tablets of stone, manna in the wilderness, or Israel gathering beneath the presence of God.
There was only a crying child.
And perhaps that is where this story becomes painfully personal.
We often want God to show us the significance of something before we obey.
Show me what this becomes.
Show me why this matters.
Show me how You will use it.
Show me the ending.
But Pharaoh’s daughter did not need to see Moses holding a staff before the crying baby was worth saving.
His life mattered while his future remained hidden.
Some of the most important acts of mercy you will ever perform may look completely ordinary when you perform them.
You may never see everything God does through the person you encouraged.
The child you protected.
The stranger you helped.
The believer you refused to abandon.
The person you forgave.
The wounded soul you listened to when everyone else had stopped listening.
The invitation to Jesus you almost kept to yourself because you were afraid someone might think you were “too religious.”
You do not know what God may do with one act of faithfulness.
But the story gets even more extraordinary.
Moses’ sister had been watching.
She approached Pharaoh’s daughter and asked whether she should find a Hebrew woman to nurse the child.
The princess agreed.
And Miriam brought Moses’ own mother.
Read the words Pharaoh’s daughter then spoke to her:
“Take this child away, and nurse it for me, and I will give thee thy wages.”
— Exodus 2:9, KJV
Do you see the reversal?
A ruler had ordered Hebrew mothers to lose their sons.
Yet through an astonishing providential turn, Moses’ own mother was given her son back for a time...
and was paid to nurse him.
The empire had declared death.
Yet the child lived.
Pharaoh wanted Hebrew sons in the Nile.
Yet the Nile became the place where Pharaoh’s daughter found the Hebrew son who would one day confront Pharaoh.
That does not mean every tragedy in this chapter suddenly became painless. Many Hebrew families suffered terribly. Biblical hope should never be used to minimize their grief.
It means Pharaoh was never sovereign over the story.
God was.
Later, when the child grew, his mother brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter.
Exodus 2:10 says:
“And he became her son. And she called his name Moses: and she said, Because I drew him out of the water.”
The Hebrew text gives the name:
מֹשֶׁה
Mosheh — Moses.
And the explanation follows:
כִּי מִן־הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִהוּ
ki min-hammayim meshitihu
“Because I drew him out of the water.”
The biblical narrator connects Moses’ name with the Hebrew verb מָשָׁה (mashah), “to draw out.”
He was the one drawn out.
And later, by God’s power, he would become the man through whom an entire people were brought out.
Not because Moses possessed some secret greatness within himself.
Not because Pharaoh’s daughter understood the whole divine plan.
Not because human courage could accomplish redemption by itself.
God was writing a story larger than any of them could see.
But there is another detail Christians cannot afford to miss.
Moses was important.
Moses was chosen.
Moses became Israel’s great human deliverer.
But Moses was never the final Deliverer.
The Bible keeps moving.
Beyond Egypt.
Beyond Sinai.
Beyond the wilderness.
Beyond Moses.
Until eventually another Child entered a world ruled by violent men.
Another ruler felt threatened.
Another slaughter of children darkened the story.
Another Child escaped death.
And that Child was Jesus Christ.
Yet Jesus did not come merely to rescue one nation from an earthly Pharaoh.
He came to confront a slavery deeper than Egypt.
Sin.
Jesus said:
“Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin.”
— John 8:34, KJV
That slavery reaches into places chains cannot touch.
Pride.
Lust.
Bitterness.
Greed.
Secret addictions.
Self-righteousness.
Hatred.
Religious hypocrisy.
The carefully maintained Christian appearance hiding a heart drifting farther and farther from Christ.
Maybe that is why you are still reading.
Perhaps everyone thinks you are doing fine.
You know the worship songs.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know how to post the verse.
You know how to smile at church.
But when the room becomes quiet and there is nobody left to impress...
you know.
Something has been drowning.
Your prayer life.
Your hunger for Scripture.
Your tenderness toward God.
Your marriage.
Your integrity.
Your hope.
Your willingness to repent.
You have learned how to keep breathing while spiritually sinking.
And somewhere along the way, you started believing that your scandal was stronger than His grace.
It isn't.
Moses was drawn from water.
Israel was drawn from Egypt.
But Jesus Christ came to accomplish the rescue to which every lesser deliverance ultimately makes us look.
At the cross, Christ did not simply offer advice to prisoners.
He gave Himself for sinners.
“For Christ also hath once suffered for sins, the just for the unjust, that he might bring us to God...”
— 1 Peter 3:18, KJV
That is the Gospel.
Not become respectable enough and maybe God will accept you.
Not hide your worst chapters and hope heaven never notices.
Not repair yourself until Jesus finally considers you worthy.
Christ died for sinners.
The righteous One for the unrighteous.
And He rose again.
Grace does not tell you that sin does not matter.
The cross proves how terribly sin matters.
Grace tells you that Jesus is greater.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
It is the sinner finally stopping the exhausting attempt to hide from the One who already sees everything.
You can come into the light.
You can confess.
You can turn.
You can surrender.
You can stop pretending.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
— 1 John 1:9, KJV
Maybe your story has a chapter you wish you could tear out.
Maybe people know what you did.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe your scandal was public.
Maybe yours lives behind a locked phone screen.
Maybe you were the one who caused the damage.
Maybe you are carrying wounds caused by someone else.
Maybe you have spent years believing the worst moment of your life deserves the final word.
Look again at the crying baby in the basket.
Then look at the man standing before Pharaoh.
The first scene did not look like the ending.
And neither does yours have to be.
But Christianity is not the promise that every earthly circumstance will turn out exactly as we want. Moses himself would suffer, fail, grieve, and eventually die outside the Promised Land.
Our hope is deeper than comfortable circumstances.
Our hope has a name.
Jesus.
He forgives.
Jesus restores.
Jesus transforms.
Jesus saves.
Jesus takes people whose stories appear irreparably stained and makes them trophies, not of human perfection, but of divine mercy.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Be truthful.
Or comment, “Christ is still healing me,” if your testimony is unfinished but you know His hands have not abandoned you.
Sometimes somebody else needs to see that they are not the only believer struggling to come home.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach at them.
Because perhaps they need reminding that the chapter they are living through is not necessarily the final chapter.

Salvation is God's gift of grace through faith in Christ, not something bought with money. But if you want to glorify God with your resources, one legitimate biblical expression of stewardship is voluntarily supporting Gospel work that is faithfully serving others.
But never confuse supporting a ministry with supporting your salvation.
You cannot purchase grace.
You cannot buy forgiveness.
Jesus already paid the price sinners could never pay.
So before you leave this article, return one final time to Egypt.
A baby is crying.
A princess is looking down.
She does not know that those tiny hands will someday carry the staff associated with signs before Pharaoh.
She does not know that those little feet will someday stand before the ruler of Egypt.
She does not know that the child she draws from the water will become the human instrument God uses in one of Scripture's greatest acts of deliverance.
She only knows there is a child in front of her.
And compassion requires a response.
Perhaps something is in front of you now too.
A person to forgive.
A sin to confess.
A relationship to repair.
A believer to encourage.
A Gospel to share.
A Christ you have admired from a distance but never truly surrendered to.
Do not demand to see the entire story before taking the next faithful step.
Pharaoh thought the river would bury Israel’s future.
God permitted a little ark to float upon those waters instead.
And long after Pharaoh’s throne disappeared into history, the story of that crying Hebrew child was still being told.
Because kings can issue decrees.
Empires can threaten.
Sin can scar.
People can fail you.
Your past can accuse you.
Shame can whisper your name in the darkness.
But none of them gets to sit on God's throne.
And when Jesus Christ takes hold of a surrendered life, your darkest chapter does not have the authority to write your final sentence.
The river that looked like the end of Moses became the place from which he was drawn—and the cross that looked like the end of Jesus became the place from which grace would call sinners home.
